name: Ferrochem Pressline Chemical Processing Rig
description:
Ferrochem's standard floor kit for pressline workers handling caustic synthesis compounds — a full-coverage rig in industrial teal with safety-orange contrast panels across the chest, upper arms, and boot caps. The outer shell is a heavyweight chembarrier-treated coverall with sealed seams, rated for Class 2 chemical splash exposure. The Ferrochem logo — a stylized double-helix inside a hexagon — is heat-pressed in reflective white on the back and left chest. The wrists terminate in deep cuff rings designed to lock with standard-issue nitrile-blend gauntlet gloves, which are tucked into a thigh utility loop when not in active use. A built-in spine channel runs the coverall's back panel, accommodating spinal augmentation rigs up to Class 3 without pinching or seal compromise. Underneath is a Pragma Systems adaptive base layer in bone white that wicks and regulates temperature through twelve-hour shifts in elevated-heat environments.

Footwear is the Varsen ChemBarrier Pull-On in teal-dyed rubber with a steel midsole and chemical-rated outsole. A full-face shield visor clips to a reinforced collar ring and hangs at the chest when not deployed. Workers typically customize the rig with handwritten name tags in paint marker over the issued name patch (the printed ones peel in three weeks), and most develop small personal tells — a colored rag tucked in the left pocket, a string of prayer beads looped through a utility ring, a sticker from a street vendor half-melted by solvent spray. This is a serious piece of protective gear worn by people who understand exactly what it protects against.
functionality: Class 2 chemical splash protection, sealed seam construction, spine channel for augmentation rigs up to Class 3, wrist cuff-lock system for gauntlet integration, full-face visor clip mount, steel midsole, temperature-regulating base layer, thigh utility loop for glove storage
what_it_says: You work with things that can dissolve your skin, and the company has decided your continued function is worth the cost of this suit. There's no glamour here, but there's competence — workers who wear this rig know their protocols cold, because the alternative is a chemical burn incident report and a week in a Lazarus clinic. The personal modifications say: I've been here long enough to have opinions.
manufacturer: Ferrochem Industries (corponation-issued); base layer by Pragma Systems
price_range: Φ310–Φ420 (issued; personal replacement Φ95–Φ150 per component)
story_hooks: A pressline worker's rig tests positive for a compound that isn't on the approved synthesis list — something is being processed in the facility that doesn't appear in any official inventory.

The sealed seams on a batch of recently issued rigs have been quietly downgraded to Class 1 protection while still being labeled Class 2 — a cost-cutting measure that someone buried in a procurement memo.
A worker's personal modification — a specific arrangement of colored rags in their utility loops — turns out to be a coded signal used by a labor organizing cell operating inside the plant.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian full-coverage chemical processing suit that reads as industrial-military on the wearer. The silhouette is blocky and functional — broad shoulders, reinforced torso, tapered legs. The dominant teal base with safety-orange accent panels creates high visibility and a distinctly corporate-issued aesthetic. The Ferrochem hexagon-helix logo in reflective white signals institutional affiliation. Overall impression: serious protective gear for hazardous work, worn by people who accept occupational risk.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and accommodating through the torso to allow layering and augmentation; tapered at wrists and ankles for seal integrity. The spine channel creates a subtle vertical emphasis down the back without restricting movement. Designed for function over fashion, but cut to allow twelve-hour wear without chafing.
physical_description.primary_material: Heavyweight chembarrier-treated nylon-blend coverall with sealed seams (Class 2 chemical splash rated). Pragma Systems adaptive base layer underneath in moisture-wicking synthetic blend. Varsen ChemBarrier rubber boots with steel midsole.
physical_description.texture: Smooth, slightly waxy outer shell (chembarrier coating); subtle ribbed texture on base layer visible at cuffs and neck; grippy rubber on boot soles and heel.
physical_description.color_scheme: Industrial teal as dominant color; safety-orange contrast panels across chest, upper arms, and boot caps; bone-white base layer at collar and wrists; reflective white logo and trim; black reinforcement stitching throughout.
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty front zip with sealed tape; deep magnetic snap cuff rings at wrists designed to lock with gauntlet gloves; pull-on boots with elasticated heel.
distinctive_features: Sealed seam construction for chemical containment
Built-in spine channel accommodating Class 3 augmentation rigs
Deep cuff rings with gauntlet glove attachment points
Utility loop on right thigh for hanging gloves during breaks
Reinforced collar ring for snap-clip visor mounting
Full-face shield visor (stores at chest when not deployed)
Ferrochem logo (double-helix in hexagon) in reflective white on back and left chest
Issued name patch (typically overwritten in paint marker)
Weathered customization: handwritten names, tucked rags, prayer beads, vendor stickers half-melted by solvent exposure
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–4 working class. Corpo-issued safety standard, not luxury, but reliable equipment issued to essential floor workers. The customization patterns reflect worker agency within strict corporate framework.
physical_description.cultural_context: Ferrochem Industries floor worker — pressline operator, chemical synthesis technician, hazmat-rated position. Wearing this marks you as blue-collar corpo: stable employment, occupational risk, institutional loyalty (or at least institutional visibility). The customizations suggest street-side resilience and peer community within the facility.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in but meticulously maintained. Outer shell shows minor solvent stains and small scuffs from equipment contact; seams remain intact. Base layer visible at cuffs is dingy from repeated washing. Name patch is hand-modified. Boots show salt stains and minor cracking in the rubber. The visor may have light scoring from chemical splash. Personal touches (prayer beads, rags, stickers) are worn but deliberately positioned.
